title: Welcome to the Nechako Watershed · Learning map
summary: A guided map through five community cases, with 25 adapted questions connecting climate, water, ecosystems and community well-being. Based on the original portal’s publicly accessible learning module.
sourceNote: PGMaps authored this summary and reworded prompts from the Nechako Watershed Portal’s Learning Module, verified without login on 2026-10-12. Original educational content remains credited to the source portal. Community coordinates come from the existing public nwsviz research-location snapshot (project_reference positions); they are approximate context markers, not field observations. The contextual watershed outlines reuse the existing Government of British Columbia Freshwater Atlas snapshot, simplified at 50 metres with topology preserved. Climate results and the original saved map workspace are not included.
details: This adaptation retains the five-place structure and ecological, social, health and Indigenous-knowledge themes of the source. It is not a verbatim copy, an answer key or the source project’s saved map.
The source publication/update date was not established. The displayed package date describes this PGMaps adaptation and public-access verification.

The map highlights the FWA Nechako named watershed within a shared Fraser/Nechako context snapshot. Community point coordinates follow the existing public research-location project; they do not identify sampling locations or legal territory boundaries.

scenes.label: Start here
scenes.title: Five places, one connected watershed
scenes.text: A PGMaps adaptation of the publicly accessible “Welcome to the Nechako Watershed” Learning Module. Explore how climate, water, ecosystems and community well-being connect across five places.
paragraphs: The original module encourages integrative thinking across ecological, social and health questions, while recognizing Indigenous knowledge and relationships with place. Prince George, Vanderhoof, Fraser Lake, Burns Lake and Fort St. James are the five stops, each with five reworded discussion prompts.

This map supplies geographic context and approximate community markers. It does not reproduce the source project’s climate surfaces, give answers, or calculate local climate impacts. Read each prompt alongside the original module and appropriate observations or datasets.
The source was checked anonymously through Links → Learning Module on October 12, 2026. That is the verification date, not the source’s publication date.

scenes.label: Prince George
scenes.title: Where rivers meet
scenes.text: Start at the meeting of the Nechako and Fraser rivers. The original module situates this case in Lheidli T’enneh territory and connects watershed conditions with an urban community.
paragraphs: 1. Compare the city’s temperature patterns with the other four communities. What could those differences mean at the river confluence?
2. Consider extreme heat alongside streets, buildings and shade. Which local conditions could intensify heat exposure?
3. Look at precipitation together with the two rivers. What additional evidence would help assess flood exposure?
4. Trace the salmon migration route through the confluence. Where could warmer water create challenges?
5. Think about swimming, fishing and boating. How could changing river conditions affect these activities?

scenes.label: Vanderhoof
scenes.title: Braided water and agricultural land
scenes.text: The source case connects the braided Nechako River near Vanderhoof with agriculture and white sturgeon habitat in Saik’uz territory. It asks readers to consider climate change alongside an already regulated river.
paragraphs: 1. Compare heat patterns at Vanderhoof with the other places. Which geographic differences deserve closer investigation?
2. Locate farmland alongside climate information. How could heat and water availability affect agricultural decisions?
3. Consider white sturgeon habitat in the braided river. Which changes in temperature and flow matter to this habitat?
4. Compare precipitation upstream and downstream. What would be needed to connect it with irrigation demand and river health?
5. Distinguish the effects of river regulation from climate change. What observations could help explain their combined influence?

scenes.label: Fraser Lake
scenes.title: Lakes and their connections
scenes.text: The original module places Fraser Lake within Stellat’en and Nadleh Whut’en territories. It follows connections among lake temperature, fisheries, surrounding forests and the Stellako River.
paragraphs: 1. Compare this lake community with other lake communities. How might air temperature connect with aquatic habitat?
2. Examine extreme heat to the east and west. Which seasonal activities on the lake could be affected?
3. Follow the Stellako connection between François Lake and Fraser Lake. What information would help explain changes along that connection?
4. Consider surrounding forests and wildfire. How might a fire affect runoff and lake water quality?
5. Begin with the importance of traditional fishing. Whose knowledge and observations are needed to understand local impacts?

scenes.label: Burns Lake
scenes.title: Fire, water and winter activities
scenes.text: The Burns Lake case brings wildfire, nearby lakes and industrial activity into one discussion. The source uses the Dakelh name Ts’il Kaz Koh and asks readers to connect climate patterns with community life.
paragraphs: 1. Compare extreme heat across the five places. How could that evidence inform questions about wildfire exposure?
2. Look at temperature and precipitation near previously burned areas, including the Shovel Lake fire. What should be checked before drawing a conclusion?
3. Compare the nearby lakes with other watershed water bodies. Which differences could shape their response?
4. Consider industrial sites and downstream water. What evidence is needed to assess runoff pathways and possible impacts?
5. Think about lake ice, recreation and transportation. What local observations would reveal changing winter conditions?

scenes.label: Fort St. James
scenes.title: A northern lake and migration route
scenes.text: The original case begins at the outlet of Stuart Lake, Nak’albun, in Nak’azdli Whut’en territory. It connects the Stuart–Takla system with salmon, forest change, winter ice and heritage experiences.
paragraphs: 1. Compare northern and southern communities in the module. Do the displayed temperature patterns support the same interpretation everywhere?
2. Examine extreme heat alongside forest composition. What changes might deserve monitoring?
3. Consider ice formation and spring melt on Stuart Lake. What records could support comparison with other lakes?
4. Trace the Stuart–Takla salmon route through the wider watershed. How might conditions vary along a migration?
5. Think about cultural and heritage visits around Nak’albun. How could changing seasons affect access and interpretation?

scenes.label: Bring it together
scenes.title: Compare places, then check the evidence
scenes.text: The useful outcome is a connected set of questions: how do conditions differ, who is affected, and which evidence could explain the differences?
paragraphs: A layer, a publication and a lived observation describe different parts of the watershed. Keep the source, time period, units and geographic extent attached to each when comparing them.

Use the source module for its full wording and teaching materials. The PGMaps research project and native portal offer separate routes to publications and available map services. A prompt about climate change is a question to investigate, not a measurement shown by this context map.
